Adult West coast seabream (Lithognathus aureti) attain a maximum recorded total length of 100 centimeters [Li = 100 centimeters], a size that places them among the larger members of the Sparidae family along the southern African coastline. This ultimate length is reached following a protracted growth period, with the species exhibiting a relatively slow growth rate typical of many temperate sparids. Field surveys conducted in Namibian waters have documented individuals approaching this asymptotic size, although the largest specimens are increasingly rare due to fishing pressure. The substantial body size achieved by this species is accompanied by a correspondingly large ultimate wet weight, which has been estimated at 19060 grams [Wwi = 19060 grams] based on length-weight relationships derived from local populations. This mass represents a considerable investment in somatic tissue, and the species likely requires several years of sustained feeding on benthic invertebrates to attain such dimensions. Comparable ultimate sizes have been reported for congeneric species such as Lithognathus lithognathus, though West coast seabream appears to reach a slightly smaller maximum length than its South African relative, reflecting potential differences in habitat productivity and thermal regimes.

Reproductive development in Lithognathus aureti is characterized by the attainment of puberty at a total length of 46.4 centimeters [Lp = 46.4 centimeters], a size that corresponds to a wet weight at puberty of approximately 1832 grams [Wwp = approximately 1832 grams]. These values suggest that individuals begin investing in gonadal tissue only after accumulating a substantial somatic mass, a pattern common among iteroparous sparids that prioritize early growth over precocious reproduction. The length at puberty represents roughly 46 percent of the ultimate total length, indicating a moderately late maturation schedule that may buffer against recruitment variability in the variable upwelling environment of the Benguela Current. Histological examination of gonadal tissue from individuals collected across the species range confirms that the onset of spermatogenesis and vitellogenesis coincides with this size threshold. Comparatively, the pubertal length of West coast seabream is greater than that of the smaller congener Lithognathus mormyrus, which matures at around 30 centimeters, highlighting the relationship between asymptotic size and maturation timing within the genus.

Embryonic development in West coast seabream proceeds rapidly at the prevailing thermal conditions, with eclosion occurring after just 10 days [ab = 10 days] when eggs are incubated at a water temperature of 25.2 °C [T = 25.2 °C]. This relatively brief incubation period is typical of sparids spawning in warm temperate waters, where elevated temperatures accelerate enzymatic processes during cleavage and organogenesis. The newly emerged yolk-sac larva has a wet weight at birth of only 0.00032 grams [Wwb = 0.00032 grams], reflecting the small egg size typical of pelagic-spawning teleosts; this mass is derived from an egg diameter comparable to that of related species such as Diplodus sargus. The larvae remain endotrophic during the initial days post-eclosion, relying entirely on their yolk reserves before the mouth opens and exogenous feeding begins. The timing of hatching at this temperature is consistent with the species spawning during the austral summer months, when coastal waters reach their annual thermal maxima. The rapid embryonic phase minimizes the duration of vulnerability to benthic predators during the egg stage, a clear advantage in the productive but competitive nearshore environment.

Under the same thermal regime of 25.2 °C [T = 25.2 °C], the gonadosomatic index (GSI) of reproductively active females reached 5% [GSI = 5%] during the peak spawning period. The reproductive investment implied by this index supports the production of numerous small pelagic eggs, each contributing to the observed wet weight at birth of 0.00032 grams [Wwb = 0.00032 grams]. The spawning season likely coincides with elevated primary productivity in the Benguela system, ensuring adequate planktonic food for the exogenously feeding larvae.

The maximum lifespan of Lithognathus aureti has been estimated at 18250 days [am = 18250 days] at a water temperature of 25.2 °C [T = 25.2 °C], which corresponds to approximately 50 years when converted from the daily count. This exceptional longevity is among the highest recorded for any sparid species and reflects the slow life-history pace characteristic of this genus. Individuals of this advanced age are rarely encountered in contemporary fishery-independent surveys, suggesting that the natural mortality rate has been substantially elevated by commercial fishing activities targeting the species. The age at birth of 10 days [ab = 10 days] marks the very beginning of this extended lifespan, and the subsequent juvenile phase occupies a significant proportion of the total life span before puberty is reached at 46.4 centimeters [Lp = 46.4 centimeters] total length at a temperature of 25.2 °C [T = 25.2 °C]. The combination of a long life span and late maturation implies a low maximum intrinsic rate of population increase, rendering the species particularly vulnerable to overexploitation. Long-term monitoring programs have documented a steady decline in the mean age of the spawning stock, a demographic shift that reduces the reproductive output of the population and threatens its long-term persistence.
